newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Cocoa - Brazil unlikely to import despite crop size.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa - Brazil unlikely to import despite crop size.

text.p: Brazil is unlikely to import cocoa beans on a large scale despite the small size of the current main crop, traders said.
Farmers last week predicted that the crop, harvested from October to April, could be as low as 800,000 60-kilo bags following two months of drought during the flowering period in June and July.
But grinders said they were well-stocked with beans and did not envisage having to import, even though local chocolate consumption is currently growing at around five percent a year.
"You may see the odd small import during January and February but nobody is going to import large volumes, it won't be necessary," said a trader.
Two years ago, Cargill imported around 5,000 tonnes of Ivorian beans to overcome a gap in local production between January and March.
However, traders said that since then the industries had become used to the new reality of falling production and had aggressively bought up the cocoa beans before the harvest dried up.
Local Brazilian chocolate production is around 300,000 tonnes a year, while the 1996/7 crop as a whole is expected to yield around 2.6 million bags 60-kilo games, around 156,000 tonnes.
Traders estimated that Brazilian chocolate manufacturers use one tonne of beans to make three tonnes of chocolate, which means that at least 50,000 tonnes would be left over for export.

Nearly all of this is destined for the countries of the Mercosul trading block -- Paraguay, Uruguay and principally Argentina -- plus Chile, the only countries which Brazil now regularly exports to, traders said.
Some dealers added they believed the main crop could still reach 1.0 million 60-kilo bags and that estimates of 800,000 were "exagerrated on the low side."
They also pointed out that the Amazon region of Brazil was expected to produce a further 20,000 tonnes in the 1996/7 crop.
"It is also normal for factories to shut down for two to four weeks in the summer, for collective holidays and to carry out maintenance," said a dealer.
